description: ESG classification prompts for sportswear brand news articles

v1.0.0.commit_message: Initial prompt version - baseline extracted from config.py
v1.0.0.description: Original ESG labeling prompts with brand verification, ESG category definitions, and false positive guidance

v1.1.0.commit_message: Add Substantive Coverage Test for clearer false positive classification
v1.1.0.description: Adds explicit guidance for identifying false positives where brand mentions are too tangential to warrant inclusion in any topical category. Clarifies that articles with superficial brand references (data tables, roundup lists, passing mentions) should be marked as false positives.

v1.2.0.commit_message: Clarify is_sportswear_brand policy for stock articles
v1.2.0.description: Clarifies that is_sportswear_brand is about substantive content, not just identity. Pure stock metrics (short interest, price movements, moving averages) with no commentary should be false_positive. Adds Finance Category Test: would this article be useful if we added a Finance category? If just raw metrics from Yahoo Finance, it's a false positive.

v1.3.0.commit_message: Add comprehensive product review guidance to prevent ESG mislabeling
v1.3.0.description: Adds critical section distinguishing product reviews, roundups, shopping articles, gift guides, and sneaker drops from corporate ESG news. Product content that mentions sustainable materials should NOT receive ESG categories - sustainability features are product marketing copy, not corporate ESG reporting. Includes examples table, key question test, and guidance on borderline product launches with ESG angle.

v1.4.0.commit_message: Add explicit guidance for comparison/analogy brand mentions as false positives
v1.4.0.description: Adds detailed guidance for identifying false positives when brands are mentioned only as comparisons, analogies, or reference points. New section covers color comparisons ('reminiscent of Nike's Infrared'), style comparisons ('Patagonia vibes'), quality references ('rivals Under Armour'), and aspiration analogies ('the Patagonia of baby clothes'). Includes quick-check question to help distinguish between articles ABOUT a brand vs articles using the brand as a reference point. Addresses cases like the Herman Miller gaming chair article that mentioned Nike only as a color comparison.
